title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A blueprint carries no inventory risk; a lump-sum construction contract carries every delay on its balance sheet.
epigraph.author: Project Economics Principle

web_blocks.text: Two Operating Engines: Consultancy & Engineering vs. Turnkey Projects

web_blocks.html: Engineers India Limited reports two main segments under Ind AS 108: Consultancy & Engineering Projects, and Turnkey Projects [13, 15]. Turnkey Projects include Lump-Sum Turnkey (LSTK) and depository-basis work [13, 15]. Both units serve energy, petrochemical, fertilizer, metal, and infrastructure clients, yet their economics differ sharply [15, 19]. In Consultancy & Engineering, EIL sells design know-how, Front-End Engineering Design (FEED), Project Management Consultancy (PMC), and EPCM man-hours [6, 15]. Only EIL's fee enters revenue, yielding segment margins of 22% to 31% [15, 20]. In Turnkey Projects, EIL handles equipment buying, fabrication, and site erection [15, 20]. Equipment and contractor costs flow through EIL's sales line, lifting revenue while keeping normal margins at 4% to 8% [15, 20].

web_blocks.caption: Standalone Segment Revenue, Profit & Margin Evolution (FY22–H1 FY27)
web_blocks.takeaway: Consultancy made up 46% of FY26 sales but 54% of segment profit (₹423.7 Cr of ₹779.8 Cr). In H1 FY27, it rose to 68% of sales and 91% of segment profit.

web_blocks.html: The standalone segment figures show why quarterly and annual results can swing sharply [19, 20]. In FY26, Turnkey sales rose 53% to ₹2,067.8 crore and earned ₹356.1 crore in segment profit [19, 20]. That 17% margin spiked due to a 38% Q3 FY26 margin from project closeouts and change-order settlements [19, 20]. In H1 FY27, those large turnkey jobs wound down, so Turnkey sales fell to ₹509.8 crore (32% of mix) [15, 20]. Turnkey margins normalized to 4%–8%, yielding ₹31.7 crore in profit [15, 20]. Meanwhile, Consultancy sales climbed to ₹1,093.4 crore (68% of mix) and earned ₹303.3 crore at a 28% margin, peaking at 31% in Q2 FY27 [15, 20].

web_blocks.text: Concrete Real-World Examples: End-to-End Execution in Both Segments

web_blocks.html: One real project from each unit shows how the two models work on site. In Consultancy & Engineering, EIL's top overseas job is the Dangote Refinery and Petrochemical Complex in Nigeria [10, 18]. In FY26–FY27, that mandate grew to add a Train-2 EPCM job (~US$360 million / ₹3,000+ crore) and a four-train fertilizer plant [10, 18]. EIL also won a ₹286 crore PMC/EPCM fertilizer contract in Ethiopia [10, 18]. On EPCM jobs, EIL runs feasibility studies, writes engineering packages, vets global vendors, and oversees site crews. The client pays suppliers and builders directly, while EIL bills only for engineering hours and oversight [15]. As a result, EIL carries low working-capital and material-cost risk, and segment margins stay at 24%–30% [15].

In Turnkey Projects (LSTK and depository work), EIL acts as prime contractor for state firms like IOCL, BPCL, HPCL, or ISPRL [5, 15]. Work covers refinery revamps, tankage terminals, and institutional buildings [5, 15]. On a turnkey package, EIL designs the unit, buys long-lead gear, hires site crews, and commissions the plant [15]. Because equipment and material costs pass through EIL's income statement, sales jump during peak site work [15, 20]. However, operating margins sit at 4%–7% during early work and only jump when final change orders settle at closeout [15, 20].

Oil refining and petrochemicals still drive most sales, yet EIL has built new verticals in infrastructure, metals, water, and clean energy [5, 10]. Recent wins include completing the Reserve Bank of India's Greenfield Data Centre and Training Institute at Bhubaneswar [10]. EIL also serves as Independent Engineer for Noida International Airport and advised on the Shri Ram Temple Complex at Ayodhya [10]. In metals, it won a project management job for Hindustan Copper's ₹7,189 crore mine expansion [10]. It is also pursuing nuclear balance-of-plant work and coal gasification studies backed by a ₹34,000 crore state viability policy [15, 18]. In clean energy, EIL is building a 5 TPD compressed biogas (CBG) plant [15, 18].

Two equity-accounted stakes and one subsidiary complete the group structure [3, 7]. Certification Engineers International Limited (CEIL), a 100% subsidiary, handles third-party audits, safety checks, and offshore certification [7]. Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Limited (RFCL) is a 26% joint venture with NFL and FCIL running a 3,850 TPD urea plant in Telangana [7, 15, 18]. After years of early losses, RFCL turned profitable in H1 FY27, adding ₹63 crore to EIL's consolidated profit (₹42 crore in Q1 and ₹20 crore in Q2) [7, 15, 18]. Finally, EIL's 4.37% stake in Numaligarh Refinery Limited (NRL) brings steady dividends, including ₹21 crore in Q2 FY27 [15, 18]. For an owner, group profit now blends high-margin fees, cyclical turnkey work, and steady JV and dividend income. Chapter 3 traces how this mix turns into unit cash flow.

Each segment carries a distinct risk profile for shareholders. In Consultancy, EIL bills for engineering hours, design reviews, and site supervision [6]. Fixed overhead stays stable, so incremental revenue drops straight to operating profit [15][20]. In Turnkey EPC, EIL buys equipment from third-party vendors and manages site subcontractors [6][19]. Margins stay thin at 4% to 8%, and unexpected site delays can quickly erode profits [20]. Watching the revenue split between these two engines explains most quarterly earnings surprises [15][19].

Geographic diversification also reshapes segment margins. Overseas consultancy jobs in Nigeria and the Middle East often carry higher billing rates per man-hour than domestic PSU contracts [8][15]. As international work scales toward 55% of the ₹20,421 Cr backlog, blended Consultancy realization improves [15][26]. However, overseas execution demands local visa compliance, foreign-currency hedging, and strict milestone sign-offs [11][17]. Monitoring regional revenue split alongside segment mix helps track this margin tailwind [14][15].

book_paragraphs: When you look at Engineers India Limited's income statement, you are actually looking at two completely different businesses wearing the same corporate badge. If you blend them together in your head, you will misread every quarterly result. Your first job as a careful analyst is to separate them cleanly: Consultancy & Engineering on one side, and Turnkey Projects on the other.

Consultancy & Engineering is a pure brainpower business. Clients hire EIL to run feasibility studies, design a refinery or petrochemical plant from concept to detailed engineering (Pre-FEED, FEED, and detailed engineering), evaluate global equipment vendors, and supervise construction as the Owner's Engineer or EPCM contractor. In this segment, EIL does not buy steel, turbines, or concrete. Only its engineering and project management fees show up as revenue, which is why Consultancy routinely earns 24% to 31% operating margins.

Turnkey Projects—what the industry calls Lump-Sum Turnkey or LSTK, alongside depository-basis execution—works on the exact opposite economics. Here, EIL takes on the procurement of plant and machinery and the management of physical site erection. Every rupee of pipe, vessel, and subcontractor labor passes through EIL's revenue line, which inflates turnover during peak construction but compresses normal margins to 4% to 8%.

book_subsections.title: Walking Through Two Real-World Projects
paragraphs: To make this concrete, picture two contracts on EIL's desk. First, imagine the Dangote Refinery expansion and fertilizer complex in Nigeria, or the new ₹286 crore fertilizer mandate in Ethiopia scheduled through May 2028. Under this EPCM consultancy model, EIL deploys process engineers from Gurugram and site supervisors to oversee the build, while Dangote writes the checks directly to equipment manufacturers and local contractors. If steel prices jump or a port shipment is delayed, EIL's margin does not get crushed by material cost overruns. That is why Consultancy generated ₹303.3 crore of segment profit on ₹1,093.4 crore of revenue in the first half of FY27—roughly 91% of all operating segment profit—even though total company revenue dipped 9% year-on-year.

Now contrast that with a domestic Turnkey package for an Indian oil marketing company, such as a refinery modernization unit, an offshore platform revamp, or a tankage terminal. EIL buys the equipment, hires the erection crews, and bills the client on percentage-of-completion milestones. During FY26, Turnkey turnover surged 53% to ₹2,067.8 crore and delivered a rare ₹356.1 crore profit because older projects closed out and change orders were settled at a 17% margin—including a 38% spike in Q3 FY26 alone. One year later, in Q2 FY27, new turnkey projects were just starting up, turnover dropped to ₹208 crore, and the segment margin snapped right back to 4%. As Finance Director Sanjay Jindal explained to analysts, early-stage turnkey projects have low cost progress and naturally book 4% to 5% margins until execution hits mid-cycle momentum. That swing is not a sign of broken management; it is the natural physics of turnkey accounting.

book_subsections.title: Beyond Oil: Data Centers, Copper, and the RFCL Turnaround
paragraphs: You should also note how EIL is stretching its engineering muscle beyond hydrocarbons. The same project-management discipline that built 20 of India's 23 refineries is now being applied to mission-critical data centers—such as the Reserve Bank of India's greenfield data center and training institute in Bhubaneswar—alongside independent-engineer roles at Noida International Airport, advisory work at the Shri Ram Temple Complex in Ayodhya, and a project management deal for Hindustan Copper's ₹7,189 crore mine expansion. EIL is also building early-stage credentials in nuclear balance-of-plant engineering, coal gasification studies backed by a ₹34,000 crore government viability policy, and a 5 TPD compressed biogas plant in Maharashtra.

Finally, look at EIL's subsidiaries and joint ventures, which add an important layer to consolidated earnings. Wholly owned subsidiary Certification Engineers International Limited (CEIL) handles third-party inspection and safety certification for offshore platforms and pipelines. Meanwhile, EIL's 26% joint venture in Ramagundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Limited (RFCL)—a 3,850 TPD gas-based urea plant in Telangana built with NFL and FCIL—dragged on consolidated profits during its early ramp-up years, but finally hit its stride in H1 FY27 by adding ₹63 crore to EIL's consolidated bottom line (₹42 crore in Q1 and ₹20 crore in Q2). Add recurring dividends from its 4.37% stake in Numaligarh Refinery (₹21 crore in Q2 FY27 alone), and you begin to see how EIL's asset-light core is supported by strategic industrial stakes. Next, let us trace how EIL actually wins this business and what ₹100 of revenue leaves behind on the income statement.

book_subsections.title: Why Segment Mix Drives Every Rupee of Operating Profit
paragraphs: To see why segment mix is the single most important operational lever at EIL, compare what happens inside the company when it books ₹100 crore of Consultancy work versus ₹100 crore of Turnkey EPC work. In Consultancy, EIL's engineers sit in Gurugram, New Delhi, Mumbai, or Abu Dhabi, producing feasibility studies, front-end engineering design, and detailed piping schematics. The primary cost is skilled engineering payroll, and operating margins regularly clear 25 to 31 percent.

In Turnkey EPC, by contrast, EIL acts as the prime contractor procuring specialized reactors, compressors, structural steel, and field erection services from subcontractors. Most of that ₹100 crore flows straight back out to equipment vendors, leaving EIL with a 4 to 8 percent margin—and even less if commodity prices or site schedules slip. That is why H1 FY27 delivered a striking paradox: consolidated revenue dipped 6.3 percent year-on-year as Turnkey billings halved, yet net profit jumped 138 percent because Consultancy climbed to 68 percent of the mix.

book_subsections.title: Walkthrough: How a Refinery Consultancy Mandate Unfolds on the Ground
paragraphs: Picture a state-owned or private refiner planning a multi-billion-dollar petrochemical complex—such as the Dangote expansion in Nigeria or a domestic IOCL residue upgradation unit. Long before a single crane arrives on site, the client hires EIL's Consultancy team to write the feasibility study and Front-End Engineering Design (FEED). Over six to twelve months, EIL process engineers simulate heat balances, select proprietary catalysts, size distillation columns, and prepare the technical bid packages that third-party equipment vendors will later quote against.

Once the client approves the capital budget, EIL transitions into Project Management Consultancy (PMC). Its engineers review thousands of vendor drawings, inspect pressure vessels at fabrication yards, and supervise pre-commissioning and safety audits. Because EIL is paid on engineering man-hours and milestone fees rather than bearing raw steel or cement price risk, this walkthrough explains why Consultancy generates 25 to 31 percent operating margins and requires minimal balance-sheet capital.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The 27-Point Margin Gap
book_callouts.text: In Q2 FY27, EIL earned a 31% margin in Consultancy and a 4% margin in Turnkey—a 27-percentage-point gap inside the same company. Whenever you hear that EIL's revenue fell 10% in a quarter, your very next question must be: which segment shrank?
